newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian trade seeks regulated rough diamond supply.
newsitem.headline: Indian trade seeks regulated rough diamond supply.

text.p: Indian diamond exporters on Monday called for a regulated supply of raw materials (roughs) to ensure the unhindered growth of the industry.

"There is a need for greater interaction between all the producing, manufacturing and consuming centres," said Praveen Pandya, chairman of the Gem and Jewellery Export Promotion Council (GJEPC), at the inauguration of a jewellery trade fair.

India is the world's largest exporter of cut and polished diamonds. It imports most of its roughs, the bulk of them coming from the powerful Central Selling Organisation (CSO) of the South African mining giant De Beers.
"Once supplies are regulated, I am sure manufacturers will pursue newer Asian, Latin American and East European markets without any fear of falling inventory prices," Pandya said.
The week-long fair was inaugurated by Nicky Oppenheimer, chairman of the CSO.
De Beers was committed to the development of the Indian market, Oppenheimer said.
"It's a very very important market for De Beers," he said.

GJEPC officials said they expected at least 300 buyers from abroad to visit the fair where gold and diamond jewellers put up 320 stalls. Pandya said that besides CSO some other players had emerged on the diamond distribution scene.

"Even if the producers continue to market separately, it is still possible to work out some kind of close co-operation within the broad framework of maintaining their individual market share," he said.

Pandya said such cooperation would ensure that manufacturing centres were no longer flooded with raw materials in some months while starving for them at other times. He said the instability the market had experienced over the last two years had given industry some anxious moments.
Apprehensions among consumers that there could be price wars had led them to shed inventories, forcing manufacturing centres to hold larger stocks, Pandya said.
"This brought a lot of pressure on prices in 1996 resulting in zero profitability," he said.
"It is essential to maintain the profitability in diamond manufacturing. This alone will ensure growth in this industry," Pandya said.
